---
order: 6
unit: challenge
title: "Challenge: punctuate the newsletter"
summary: "Nib typed the school fair newsletter with no punctuation at all. Students put the marks back in four parts: apostrophes, commas, colons and semicolons, then a whole paragraph, and then check the commas in a piece of their own writing."
language: maths
node: [AC9E6LA09 n3]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "The comma comes before the speech, after the words that introduce it." }
hook: "A newsletter with every fact right and not one mark of punctuation. Can you make it readable again?"
---
Nib typed the school fair newsletter fast, and the punctuation got left out. You will put it back in four parts, using the marks from this course: apostrophes, commas, colons and semicolons, and then a whole paragraph. A last step asks you to check the commas in your own writing.

## Predict: which mark first?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Thinking about which mark the newsletter needs most makes students link each job to its mark before fixing."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Nib's newsletter has a list, an opening clause and a quotation. Which one mark do all three of those need?"
  options: ["The comma", "The colon", "The semicolon", "The apostrophe"]
  actual: "The comma. It separates list items, follows an opening clause and comes before the quotation. The colon and the semicolon each do one of these jobs at most, and the apostrophe does none of them."
```

## Part 1: apostrophes

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Choosing the owner word and the contraction applies the first lesson's marks to the newsletter."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#apostrophes", height: 360 }
hint: ["Who owns the room, and how many owners are there?", "Is each gap a short form of two words, or a word that shows who owns something?"]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose the word for each gap.", when: "n_gaps_right = 3", explain: "The room belongs to all the teachers, so the apostrophe goes after the s. It's is short for it is. One stall belongs to Ava and Ben together, so the apostrophe goes on the last name." }
```

## Part 2: commas

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Choosing commas across the three jobs and a place where none belongs applies the comma lesson to the newsletter."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#commas", height: 420 }
hint: ["Name the structure in each sentence: opening phrase or clause, list, speech.", "Is any gap between a subject and its verb?"]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose a comma or no comma for each box.", when: "n_right = 5 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "A comma follows each long opening phrase or clause, separates the first items in a list and comes before the speech. 'The new library' stays joined to 'opens'." }
```

## Part 3: colons and semicolons

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Choosing among a colon, a semicolon, a comma and no mark makes students test what stands on each side."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#colons", height: 440 }
hint: ["Could each side of the gap stand alone as a sentence?", "Is the part before the gap a whole sentence that promises something?"]
check: { type: board, text: "Choose the mark for each box.", when: "n_right = 5 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "A colon follows a whole clause that promises a list or a reason. A semicolon joins two related main clauses. A comma follows an opening clause. After 'need' the clause is unfinished, so no mark." }
```

## Part 4: punctuate a whole paragraph

Copy this paragraph into your own document. It has no punctuation and no capital letters after the first word, so you will add them.

> The school fair is on Saturday Mrs Tran our principal will open it at ten When the gates open the first stall to fill will be the cake stall Last year the cakes sold out by noon this year we are baking more Ravi said we will need three things flour eggs and sugar

Punctuate it. Put in the capital letters and full stops first. Then add at least four commas, a colon and speech marks around what Ravi said.

Here is one model, so you can compare after you have tried: "The school fair is on Saturday. Mrs Tran, our principal, will open it at ten. When the gates open, the first stall to fill will be the cake stall. Last year the cakes sold out by noon; this year we are baking more. Ravi said, 'We will need three things: flour, eggs and sugar.'"

Then swap with a partner. Point to every mark and say its job. Where you chose differently, talk about which version reads better.

```step
stage: make
insight: "Punctuating a whole paragraph makes students decide each mark in context, as they do in extended writing."
hint: ["Where does each sentence end? Put the capital letters and full stops in first.", "Read it aloud. Where does your voice stop, and where does a reader need help to follow the meaning?"]
check: { type: reflect, text: "I punctuated the paragraph with capital letters, full stops, at least four commas, a colon and speech marks, and a partner and I named the job of each mark." }
```
## In your own writing

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Checking the commas in a piece of their own writing is the transfer step for the whole course."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I read a piece of my own writing for commas, found a place where one was missing or did not belong, and fixed it." }
```

## Wider: edit a partner's writing

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Editing a partner's writing for commas applies the same checks at the same level to someone else's text."
check: { type: reflect, text: "I checked a partner's writing for commas, found one to fix and explained to them which job it does or does not do." }
```

```teacher
summary: "Students put the punctuation back into Nib's school fair newsletter in
  four parts: apostrophes, commas, colons and semicolons, and then a whole
  paragraph. They finish by checking the commas in a piece of their own
  writing."
time: 50
timing: Predict 3 min · Parts 1 to 3 18 min · Part 4 12 min · Own writing 10 min
  · Wider 7 min
goals:
  - I can use apostrophes for owners and short forms.
  - I can use commas for lists, opening clauses and speech.
  - I can use a colon or a semicolon where a whole clause stands on each side.
  - I can find and fix a comma problem in my own writing.
struggle: In Part 4 students add marks everywhere, or only full stops. Ask them
  to name each comma's job aloud. If they cannot, they take the comma out.
before: >
  Do Parts 1 to 3 yourself and punctuate the Part 4 paragraph.


  This is the AC9E6LA09 node 3 challenge: commas used accurately in extended
  writing, with at least two of the three jobs (lists, separating a dependent
  clause, dialogue) and self-editing. The other marks in the course are in the
  boards too.


  The boards check marks with a clear answer. Dashes and brackets are style
  choices (an aside can sit in commas, dashes or brackets), so no board item
  depends on them. Students may use them in Part 4.


  Part 4 starts from a paragraph with no punctuation at all, shown in the lesson
  text. Students copy it into their own document and punctuate it there; the
  site does not take or check what they write. A model is shown for comparison,
  and a partner checks, or you do.


  The wider step is peer editing, which the node's wider width names. It is the
  same level, not a harder one.


  The newsletter is made up for the lesson.
running:
  - "Predict: let students argue for a mark before the answer."
  - "Parts 1 to 3: ask 'what is on each side of the gap?'"
  - "Part 4: pairs read the paragraph aloud, and one student names each mark's
    job."
  - "Own writing: students edit a real piece from another subject."
stuck:
  - see: A student puts a comma after 'Ravi' in 'Ravi said we will need...'
    ask: What is the comma for?
    fix: The comma comes after 'said', before the speech. Between a subject and its
      verb there is none.
  - see: A student leaves out the colon after 'three things'.
    ask: Is 'Ravi said we will need three things' a whole clause? What does it
      promise?
    fix: The clause promises a list. A colon introduces it.
stretch: Swap your punctuated paragraph with a partner who used dashes where you
  used commas. Whose version reads better, and why?
support: Ask students to punctuate one sentence at a time and read it aloud
  before moving to the next.
leads: >
  This ends Punctuation for meaning. Later phases return to punctuation in
  longer texts.
exit:
  q: "Punctuate: On the last day of term our class visited the museum Ava asked
    can we see the dinosaurs"
  a: On the last day of term, our class visited the museum. Ava asked, 'Can we see
    the dinosaurs?'
explain: >
  Put each mark where its job is: apostrophes for owners and short forms, commas
  for lists, opening clauses and speech, colons and semicolons for whole
  clauses.


  Read the paragraph aloud and name each mark's job.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: How do you know a mark belongs?
    prompts:
      - Pick a mark in your paragraph. What is its job?
      - What would the reader lose if it were missing?
    notes: Every mark has a job in the structure. If it has none, take it out.
  activities:
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: Name each mark
      minutes: 8
      do: >
        Partners swap paragraphs and point to every mark, saying its job. Where
        a partner cannot say, they discuss whether it belongs.
      notes: Accept dashes or brackets for an aside, and ask which reads better.
  questions:
    - at: make
      title: Which is best?
      type: question
      q: Which sentence is punctuated best?
      options:
        - Ravi said 'We need, flour, eggs and sugar.'
        - Ravi said, 'We need flour, eggs and sugar.'
        - Ravi said; 'We need flour eggs and sugar.'
      answer: 1
      explain: A comma comes before the speech and between the first items of the list.
```
